title: Being and Existence
description: What does it mean for something to exist? Ontology from Aristotle to the present

concepts.title: What Is Metaphysics?
concepts.contentHtml:
Metaphysics is the branch of philosophy that studies the most fundamental features of reality: what kinds of things exist, what they are like at their deepest level, and how they relate to each other.

The term comes from Andronicus of Rhodes' title for Aristotle's works 'after the Physics' (ta meta ta physika). Aristotle called it first philosophy — the study of being as such, prior to all the special sciences.

Central questions include: What is it for something to exist? Are there abstract objects like numbers? What makes two things the same thing at different times? Does the past still exist? Can you be the same person you were ten years ago?

concepts.title: Substance and Categories
concepts.contentHtml:
Aristotle argued that reality is structured into substances — individual things like Socrates or this tree — which are the fundamental units of being. Properties, relations, and quantities depend on substances; they do not exist on their own.

Aristotle's ten categories classified how things can be: substance, quantity, quality, relation, place, time, position, state, action, and passion. Every meaningful statement fits one category.

Kant later argued that the categories are not features of reality but of the mind — the formal structures through which experience is organised. This moved metaphysics from world-description to mind-description, a revolution in the discipline.

concepts.title: Existence and Essence
concepts.contentHtml:
Medieval philosophers asked: what is the difference between that something exists and what it is?

Aquinas distinguished existence (esse) from essence (essentia): essence is what a thing is; existence is the act of being. In God alone are essence and existence identical — God's essence just is to exist. Everything else is contingent: it has an essence but need not have existed.

Existentialists inverted the priority: Sartre's 'existence precedes essence' claims humans have no fixed essence — we create ourselves through choices. There is no human nature that precedes or constrains our self-making. This was a radical departure from Aristotelian teleology.

title: Identity and Change
description: What makes things the same over time? Personal identity and the Ship of Theseus

concepts.title: The Ship of Theseus
concepts.contentHtml:
The Ship of Theseus is one of the oldest puzzles about identity over time. The ship's planks are gradually replaced until no original plank remains. Is it still the same ship?

Hobbes sharpened the puzzle: suppose someone collects all the original planks and reassembles them. Now there are two ships — which is the original? The puzzle reveals that our intuitions about identity rely on competing criteria: continuity of parts, continuity of function and history, and spatio-temporal continuity — and these criteria can come apart.

This puzzle applies directly to bodies, organisms, institutions, and persons. What makes you the same person you were as a child?

concepts.title: Personal Identity
concepts.contentHtml:
Locke argued personal identity consists in psychological continuity — specifically, memory. You are the same person as your past self insofar as you can remember their experiences. This divorces personal identity from bodily identity.

Hume denied there is any persistent self: introspecting, he found only 'a bundle of perceptions,' never a unifying self. Personal identity is a useful fiction, not a metaphysical fact.

Parfit's Reasons and Persons (1984) argued personal identity is not what matters: what matters is psychological continuity and connectedness, which can hold in degrees and branches. In teleporter or fission cases, the question 'is it still me?' may have no determinate answer — and that's fine.

concepts.title: Properties and Universals
concepts.contentHtml:
When two roses are both red, what makes this true? Do they share a real entity — the universal redness — or only resemble each other?

Realism about universals: universals genuinely exist and are shared by particulars that instantiate them (Plato's Forms; Armstrong's immanent universals).

Nominalism: only particulars exist; 'redness' is just a word we apply to similar things. Trope theory modifies this: each red thing has its own individual redness-trope, numerically distinct but qualitatively similar.

The debate matters for understanding laws of nature, causal powers, and what it means for properties to be real features of the world rather than convenient labels.

title: Time and Modality
description: The nature of time, necessity, and possible worlds

concepts.title: A-Theory vs B-Theory of Time
concepts.contentHtml:
Does time flow, or is that an illusion? Two major views divide the metaphysics of time:

A-theory (here in its strongest form, presentism; other A-theories such as the growing block also treat the present as privileged): only the present moment genuinely exists. The past was real; the future will be real; but only now is real. 'Now' is an objective, privileged moment. Time flows as the present advances.

B-theory (eternalism / four-dimensionalism): all moments in time are equally real. The universe is a four-dimensional spacetime block. There is no objective 'now' — 'now' is indexical like 'here'. Past, present, and future events all exist.

Relativity theory favours B-theory, since simultaneity is frame-relative and there is no absolute present. Yet A-theory matches our phenomenal experience of time passing.

concepts.title: Possible Worlds and Modality
concepts.contentHtml:
Philosophers speak of what is necessarily true (true in all possible worlds), possibly true (true in some possible world), and contingently true (true in some but not all).

David Lewis defended modal realism: possible worlds are concrete realities, as real as the actual world. They are just spatiotemporally isolated from us. 'Necessarily P' means P holds in every one of these concrete worlds.

Plantinga's actualism: possible worlds are abstract objects — maximal consistent sets of propositions, or states of affairs. Only the actual world concretely exists; others are abstract representational constructs.

Modal realism is elegant but ontologically extravagant. Actualism is sparse but must explain how abstract worlds do their explanatory work.

concepts.title: Essence and Necessity — Kripke's Revolution
concepts.contentHtml:
Saul Kripke's Naming and Necessity (1980) transformed how philosophers think about essence and necessity.

Kripke argued that names are rigid designators — they refer to the same individual in every possible world. 'Aristotle' refers to the same man in all worlds where he exists.

This enabled an account of a posteriori necessity: 'Water is H₂O' is necessarily true (could not be otherwise), yet discovered empirically. Essence is not a matter of how we describe something but of what it fundamentally is.

Kripke also argued that 'pain' and 'C-fibre firing' are both rigid designators, so if pain were C-fibre firing the identity would have to be necessary; since it seems it could have been otherwise, this fuelled a powerful argument against mind-brain identity theories. His work renewed metaphysics as a serious a posteriori enterprise.

title: Free Will and Determinism
description: Can we be free in a deterministic universe?

concepts.title: The Problem of Free Will
concepts.contentHtml:
Determinism: every event, including every human decision, is causally necessitated by prior events and laws of nature. Given the complete state of the universe at any moment, all future states are fixed.

The problem: if determinism is true, my choices are the inevitable output of prior causes I did not choose. How can I be morally responsible for actions I couldn't have done otherwise?

The Consequence Argument (van Inwagen): the consequences of laws of nature and past events are not up to us; our actions are consequences of laws and past events; therefore our actions are not up to us. Free will requires the ability to do otherwise — and determinism eliminates this.

concepts.title: Compatibilism
concepts.contentHtml:
Compatibilists argue that free will and determinism are compatible. What we care about — acting from our own reasons, without compulsion or coercion — is compatible with determinism.

Hume and Hobbes were early compatibilists. If I act from my own desires and am not coerced, I act freely — regardless of whether those desires were themselves determined.

Frankfurt cases (Harry Frankfurt): a neuroscientist could intervene if you were about to choose differently, but since you choose as they want, they never intervene. You couldn't have done otherwise, yet we still hold you responsible. This suggests 'could have done otherwise' is not required for moral responsibility.

P.F. Strawson's 'Freedom and Resentment' (1962): responsibility is grounded in the reactive attitudes (resentment, gratitude) of participants in personal relationships — these don't require metaphysical libertarian freedom.

concepts.title: Libertarian Free Will and Hard Determinism
concepts.contentHtml:
Libertarians about free will (not political libertarians) hold that genuine free will exists and is incompatible with determinism — so determinism must be false or not apply to human agency.

Agent causation (Roderick Chisholm): persons as agents initiate causal chains that are not themselves caused by prior events. Critics ask how agent causation differs from randomness.

Indeterminism (quantum events) doesn't straightforwardly rescue libertarianism — a random quantum event doesn't give us control; it just makes action unpredictable.

Hard determinism accepts incompatibilism and determinism, concluding free will is illusory — along with moral responsibility, desert, and punishment. Derk Pereboom's 'hard incompatibilism' embraces these consequences while arguing society can maintain justice without desert-based punishment.

title: Grounding, Causation, and the Limits of Metaphysics
description: What explains what? Contemporary debates about the structure of reality

concepts.title: Causation
concepts.contentHtml:
Causation is everywhere in our thinking, yet notoriously hard to analyse.

Hume argued we never perceive causation directly — only the regular succession of events. Causation is a psychological habit, not a feature of the world. There is no observable 'necessary connection.'

Counterfactual analysis (Lewis): C causes E iff if C hadn't occurred, E wouldn't have. This captures much of our causal thinking but struggles with overdetermination (two simultaneous fires each independently sufficient to burn the barn).

Mechanistic accounts: causation is transmission of energy or conserved quantities through physical processes. Better for science, but may not capture all causation (negative causation: 'the absence of water caused the plant to die').

concepts.title: Grounding and Fundamentality
concepts.contentHtml:
Contemporary metaphysics is preoccupied with grounding: a non-causal explanatory relation that says what makes something the case.

The fact that this flower is red is grounded in micro-physical facts about its surface reflectance properties. The wrongness of an act is grounded in its natural features (naturalism). Mathematical truths (if real) are not caused by anything but may be grounded in structural facts about the world.

Jonathan Schaffer argues everything is grounded in a single fundamental entity: the whole universe (priority monism). Others (pluralists) hold there are many ungrounded fundamental facts. The debate echoes ancient disputes between monists (Parmenides, Spinoza) and pluralists (Democritus, Leibniz).

concepts.title: The Limits and Revival of Metaphysics
concepts.contentHtml:
Logical positivists (Carnap, Ayer) declared metaphysical claims meaningless: genuine statements must be empirically verifiable or analytically true. 'The Absolute is beyond space and time' says nothing factual.

Yet metaphysics survived and flourished. Quine's 'ontological commitment' asked: what entities must we assume exist for our best scientific theories to be true? This made metaphysics continuous with science.

Today analytic metaphysics is highly technical: applying logical tools, modal logic, and formal ontology to questions about mereology (parts and wholes), persistence, truthmakers, and laws of nature.

Critics (Ladyman, Ross) argue much 'neo-scholastic' metaphysics is disconnected from physics. The tension between armchair metaphysics and naturalistic deference to science remains live and unresolved.
